To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
youth perceive themselves as being well prepared for the world of work, and that their perceptions are not in line with the views of employers.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the ways in which the skills debate and its attendant policy and practice implications are constructed and interpreted by young people, and the ways in which these constructions influence young people's perceptions of themselves as workers and citizens.
the ways in which the concept of skills has become central to the discourse of economic restructuring, and the ways in which it is used to construct and position young people in the labour market.
the ways in which the notion of employability skills is used in the context of the youth labour market.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the skills debate is a complex and multifaceted one, and that the new Australian employabilities framework is a useful starting point for the discussion of the issue.
youth are not prepared to meet the demands of a skills‐short economy, and that the employability skills framework does little to clarify the situation.
the employability skills framework is a useful tool for employers, but that the term ‘employability skills’ is misleading, and that it should be re‐named ‘life skills’.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the new Australian employable skills framework is a step in the right direction in terms of promoting a broader understanding of the nature of the skills required by young people in transition.
it is important that we have a better understanding of the skills and attributes that young people bring to the labour market.

we are not only interested in what employers look for, we are also interested in how youth perceive their own employability skills, how they are prepared for the labour market and what they need to do in order to be more competitive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need for a more holistic approach to youth employment.

the skills debate is a distraction and a red herring, and that the focus of youth policy should not be on the acquisition of skills, whether they be hard or soft, but rather the development of the individual and the capacity to be a lifelong learner and to be resilient.
the skills shortage is not just a problem of the economy, it is also a problem of education and training, and of the socialization of young people.
